proposed_concept.title: Workflows and Process Integration Working Group
proposed_concept.description: AAIF technical working group establishing shared workflow execution models, common terminology, reference architectures, and enterprise integration patterns for AI agents.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Workflows and Process Integration Working Group (WG Workflows & Process Integration) develops vendor-neutral execution models, taxonomy, and reference architectures governing the integration of AI agents into automated workflows and enterprise systems [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7]. The group is co-chaired by Yaron Schneider (Diagrid) and Adam Seligman (Workato) [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7].

In August 2026, the group delivered the Phase One Core Terms draft, becoming the first working group in the Agentic AI Foundation to ship a formally voted asset [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7].

# Architecture / Specification

The working group organizes its technical agenda across three primary workstreams [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7]:

- **Reference Architectures**: Standardizes foundational interaction patterns for agent execution. Completed items include core architecture principles and contributing guidelines (via PR #27) as well as the "human-approved operation" architecture (`architectures/single-agent-human-approval`). A second reference architecture, "bounded autonomous remediation" (`architectures/bounded-autonomous-remediation`), covers internal agent remediation with limit escalation [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7]. Architectural fit is evaluated against an inventory using a four-outcome method: validated, partial, candidate, or no fit [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7].
- **Taxonomy**: Harmonizes workflow definitions. The Phase One Core Terms established "activity" over "step" as the foundational non-circular primitive from which "workflow" is composed [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7]. Gate, check, and evaluation vocabulary is explicitly out of scope, deferred to related groups such as [Security and Privacy](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md) and [Accuracy and Reliability](../working-groups/accuracy-and-reliability.md) [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7].
- **Critical Use Cases**: Maintains a catalog of real-world enterprise agent scenarios categorized across cohorts including human-approved operations, bounded remediation, and exception detection/escalation [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7].

# Lifecycle History

- **August 2026**: Phase One Core Terms formally approved by plenary vote [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7]. Reference Architecture deliverable locked to two architectures plus principles and contributing guides [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7]. Established a standing rule capping pull requests at roughly 10 files [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-922f59c26329-f75096f7].

proposed_concept.title: Accuracy and Reliability Working Group Survey
proposed_concept.description: Platform-neutral 16-question evaluation instrument measuring production deployment stages, failure frequencies, recovery patterns, and priorities for agent reliability.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Accuracy and Reliability Working Group Survey is a platform-neutral evaluation instrument authored by [Accuracy and Reliability](../working-groups/accuracy-and-reliability.md) to collect empirical data on how organizations deploy, measure, and stabilize production agent systems [^evt-wg-accuracy-and-reliability-pr-9].

The survey is composed of 16 questions structured across five thematic sections, specifying response logic, required input behaviors, screen-out paths, and write-in fields [^evt-wg-accuracy-and-reliability-pr-9].

# Architecture / Specification

The survey's structural sections and logic are organized as follows [^evt-wg-accuracy-and-reliability-pr-9]:

- **Eligibility (Q1)**: Initial screening gate directing disqualified respondents through three dedicated early-exit thank-you routes.
- **About the System (Q2–Q5)**: Contextual characterization of the agent workload. Q2 provides closed choices alongside a mandatory free-text "Something else" field. Q5 is optional.
- **Benefits and Challenges (Q6–Q8)**: Assessment of realized benefits and implementation friction. Q6 includes five fixed options, including "Not sure".
- **Accuracy and Reliability (Q9–Q13)**: Evaluation of failure modes, validation gates, and recovery mechanisms. Q10 includes five choices, including "Not sure".
- **Future Priorities (Q14–Q16)**: Industry and technical priority rankings, with Q16 marked optional.

All questions except Q5 and Q16 require explicit answers [^evt-wg-accuracy-and-reliability-pr-9].

# Lifecycle History

- **August 2026**: Merged initial platform-neutral specification via PR #9 along with Google Forms prototype verification [^evt-wg-accuracy-and-reliability-pr-9].

proposed_concept.description: AAIF technical working group establishing vendor-neutral agent telemetry standards, cross-boundary tracing models, and behavioral evaluation frameworks.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Observability & Traceability Working Group (WG O&T) is an Agentic AI Foundation technical working group chartered to define vendor-neutral agent telemetry standards, cross-boundary distributed tracing frameworks, and behavioral execution models [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b]. The working group is co-chaired by Pavan Sudheendra (Cisco) and Matthew Lee (Datadog) [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].

WG O&T coordinates directly with external standards bodies—including OpenTelemetry GenAI SIG, W3C Trace Context, OWASP AOS, and Agent Trace—as well as internal AAIF working groups covering Identity and Trust, Security and Privacy, and Workflows and Process Integration [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-18].

# Architecture / Specification

The working group organizes its technical initiatives into core focus tracks and workstreams [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b]:

- **Agent Behavior Trace Model**: Scope confirmed in August 2026 under the leadership of Matthew Lee, utilizing portable telemetry context to preserve causal relationships across agents, SDKs, gateways, and backends alongside OpenTelemetry GenAI [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b]. Evaluation follows an adopt, extend, or new-specification decision matrix [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-19].
- **Cross-Boundary Observability**: Developing metadata propagation mappings across agent-to-skill, skill-to-tool, agent-to-agent (A2A), and agent-to-MCP protocol boundaries, accompanied by local CLI and MCP server proposals [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].
- **Trust Pipeline Observability**: Standardizing telemetry for the Agent Resource Discovery (ARD) lifecycle spanning discovery, identity verification, policy evaluation, and execution spans [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].
- **Taxonomy Integration**: Developing and submitting definitions for agent observability terms, including Reasoning, Agent Trajectory, Context Propagation, Memory Access, Context Assembly, Retrieval, and Traceability in coordination with the [Taxonomy & Landscape Working Group](../working-groups/taxonomy-and-landscape.md) [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].

# Lifecycle History

In August 2026, WG O&T merged its Working Methods, full-stack tracing landscape survey, and prior-work updates [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b]. The Orchestration & Coordination track (Multi-Agentic Observability) was consolidated into the full working group plenary, and a formal liaison tracker (`LIAISON_TRACKER.md`) was instituted to monitor cross-WG and external standard dependencies [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b] [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-18].

proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Security & Privacy Working Group (WG S&P) is an Agentic AI Foundation technical working group chartered to develop open threat modeling frameworks, defensive architecture patterns, and baseline security practices for agentic AI architectures [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f]. The working group is chaired by Alexander Frazer (Runlayer) and Junjie Bu (Google) [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f].

# Architecture / Specification

The working group drives four core workstreams [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f]:

- **Agentic AI Threat Modeling Gap Analysis**: Led by Alon Mazor and Fernando Lucktemberg, this effort analyzes OWASP Top 10 for Agentic systems, MITRE ATLAS, CSA MAESTRO, and NIST AI RMF, while examining alignment with STRIDE and PASTA methodologies and addressing MCP and user-to-agent (HUA) considerations [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f].
- **Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide**: Authored by Fernando Lucktemberg and Matthew Khouzam, providing actionable security controls across runtime isolation, credential boundaries, and agent-user interactions [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f].
- **Security and Privacy Design Patterns Catalog**: Led by Dan Kommatas and Sagar Dashora, defining reusable, verifiable architectural safety patterns [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f].
- **Cross-WG Review Checklist**: Led by Govindaraj Palanisamy, establishing a review checklist and overlap matrix across all AAIF working groups to evaluate incoming deliverables for security and privacy risks [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f].

# Lifecycle History

In August 2026, WG S&P adopted a policy making past meeting recordings publicly accessible by default [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f]. The WG submitted a governance query to the [Technical Committee](../governance/technical-committee.md) seeking clarification regarding cross-working group ownership of protocol security stemming from the A2A donation [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-pr-22]. Coordination is also maintained with the [Taxonomy & Landscape Working Group](../working-groups/taxonomy-and-landscape.md) to define foundational agent security terms [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-922f59c26329-785b273f].

proposed_concept.title: Agent Behavior Trace Model
proposed_concept.description: Standardized telemetry context and correlation framework capturing causal relationships, execution spans, and decision outcomes across agent runtimes.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Agent Behavior Trace Model is a telemetry standard and correlation framework developed by the [Observability & Traceability Working Group](../working-groups/observability-and-traceability.md) [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b]. It uses portable telemetry context to preserve causal execution relationships across heterogeneous agents, SDKs, intermediate gateways, and telemetry backends [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].

Rather than serving as a distinct or competing model to OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, portable telemetry context complements existing distributed tracing standards by capturing multi-agent causality and execution context without requiring raw chain-of-thought capture [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].

# Architecture / Specification

The trace model addresses several distinct operational requirements [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b] [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-19]:

- **Portable Telemetry Context**: Binds context across distributed layers, ensuring identity and task tracking survive protocol hops across gateways (such as [AgentGateway](../resources/agentgateway.md)) and multi-agent coordination pipelines [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].
- **Decision and Plan Attribution**: Links plans and intermediate decisions to concrete tool execution spans and final outcomes while respecting privacy and preventing exposure of raw prompt reasoning traces [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].
- **Canonical Identifiers & Long-Running Tasks**: Enforces canonical session, task, and execution identifiers capable of resuming across durable pauses and asynchronous agent handoffs [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].
- **Evaluation and Recommendation Strategy**: Evaluated against candidate standards through a decision matrix (adopt existing, extend standard, or author new specification) informed by prior-work surveys and gap analyses [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-19].

# Lifecycle History

In August 2026, WG O&T finalized the model's initial scope and scheduled reference library development and synthetic conformance testing for September 2026 led by Matthew Lee [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b]. Target reference architectures from the [Workflows & Process Integration Working Group](../working-groups/workflows-and-process-integration.md) were identified as realistic end-to-end test cases [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-922f59c26329-f5c1b95b].

proposed_concept.title: Attested Isolated Runtime
proposed_concept.description: Architectural security pattern isolating policy evaluation and evidence signing inside hardware-attested enclaves while keeping primary agent logic outside.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Attested Isolated Runtime pattern isolates runtime policy enforcement, verdict evaluation, and cryptographic evidence signing within a hardware-attested trusted execution environment (TEE), keeping the primary agent workload outside the enclave boundary [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb]. By decoupling policy enforcement from operator host privileges, the pattern ensures that relying parties can independently verify execution integrity even when the underlying host, hypervisor, or infrastructure operator is untrusted [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].

Also known as a TEE-isolated agent runtime, confidential agent execution, or an attested enclave gateway, this pattern addresses scenarios where an agent processes confidential or regulated data in third-party environments [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].

# Architecture / Specification

The pattern establishes distinct multi-organizational roles and operational constraints across four participants [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb]:

- **Data owner:** Requires that task inputs and context are not exposed during processing [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].
- **Agent operator:** Executes the agentic workload across external or hybrid cloud compute [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].
- **Infrastructure operator:** Controls the underlying host platform, hypervisors, and scheduling layers [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].
- **Relying party:** Evaluates execution integrity and policy adherence without direct inspection capability [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].

### Core Mechanisms

1. **External Enforcement Separation:** Rather than executing complex LLM harnesses inside constrained TEEs, policy evaluation points are isolated in the enclave while the agent runs outside [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].
2. **Enclave Key Generation:** Cryptographic signing keys are generated strictly inside the attested boundary, directly binding evidence artifacts to immutable hardware measurements [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].
3. **Policy Sealing:** Governance policies are sealed against hardware launch measurements and unlocked only upon valid appraisal by an attestation verifier [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].
4. **Verifiable Telemetry and Evidence:** Emits signed evidence records per unit of execution, enabling external verification via independent appraisal [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb].

# Lifecycle History

Contributed as an initial design draft within the Security and Privacy Working Group's privacy-preserving execution workstream [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d74b6b55d493-0ef833eb]. Related runtime isolation approaches and sandboxing tooling include [resources/nono](../resources/nono.md) and related specifications such as [standards/evidence-record-spec](../standards/evidence-record-spec.md) [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].

proposed_concept.title: Submission Analyser
proposed_concept.description: Headless Flue 2.0 agent running in GitHub Actions that analyses repository issues and publishes reports, incorporating dual-matrix dry-run canary verification.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Submission Analyser is a headless agent built on Flue 2.0 and automated via GitHub Actions to inspect intake repository issues, apply structured rubric assessments, and generate evaluation summaries [^evt-submission-analyser-file-4b56c7c159ef-381bcc10].

To manage upstream LLM provider volatility, the analyser incorporates a daily dry-run canary workflow verifying both primary and fallback model pipelines across real model endpoints without performing publication actions [^evt-submission-analyser-file-4b56c7c159ef-381bcc10].

# Architecture / Specification

### Model Canary Verification

The canary workflow (`canary.yml`) isolates model availability risks from production analysis pipelines [^evt-submission-analyser-file-4b56c7c159ef-381bcc10]:

- **Dual Matrix Execution:** Evaluates both primary and fallback model legs independently with `fail-fast: false`, ensuring a failure in the primary model does not mask a silent outage in the fallback engine [^evt-submission-analyser-file-4b56c7c159ef-381bcc10].
- **Dry-Run Confinement:** Operates with `DRY_RUN=1` and minimal permissions (`contents: read`, `issues: read`, `copilot-requests: write`), explicitly excluding downstream write credentials (such as Google Drive or Discord secrets) to limit security exposure [^evt-submission-analyser-file-4b56c7c159ef-381bcc10].
- **Token Attestation:** Uses repository workflow identity tokens rather than personal access tokens (PATs) to authenticate against individual Copilot endpoints, avoiding permission revocation issues [^evt-submission-analyser-file-4b56c7c159ef-381bcc10].
- **Scheduled Frequency:** Scheduled off-peak daily (07:15 UTC) against a fixed reference issue to detect header or credential drifts prior to production triage [^evt-submission-analyser-file-4b56c7c159ef-381bcc10].

# Lifecycle History

Deployed across foundation repositories for automated issue intake analysis alongside guidelines documented in [skills/issue-analysis](../skills/issue-analysis.md) and [guidelines/working-group-submission-guidelines](../guidelines/working-group-submission-guidelines.md) [^evt-submission-analyser-file-4b56c7c159ef-381bcc10].

proposed_concept.description: Technical working group establishing threat models, defensive architecture patterns, runtime sandboxing standards, and security best practices for AI agents.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Security and Privacy Working Group is an Agentic AI Foundation technical body developing defensive reference architectures, runtime sandboxing patterns, threat classification models, and operational security guidelines for autonomous agents [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].

The group coordinates horizontal reviews with partner initiatives including [working-groups/observability-and-traceability](../working-groups/observability-and-traceability.md) and [working-groups/identity-and-trust](../working-groups/identity-and-trust.md) while maintaining active workstreams in best practices, threat modeling, and design patterns [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].

# Architecture / Specification

### Governance and Workstreams

- **Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide:** Living foundational deliverable merged via PR #9, maintained under mandatory review by designated leads [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821]. See [guidelines/agentic-ai-security-best-practices](../guidelines/agentic-ai-security-best-practices.md).
- **Threat Modeling:** Focuses on framework gap analyses interleaving weekly or bi-weekly cadence with best practices discussions [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].
- **Design Patterns Catalog:** Authors architectural blueprints for agent execution isolation, including [patterns/attested-isolated-runtime](../patterns/attested-isolated-runtime.md) [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].
- **Taxonomy Alignment:** Coordinates definition reviews for security terms (such as agent sabotage and mishandling) with the [working-groups/taxonomy-and-landscape](../working-groups/taxonomy-and-landscape.md) group [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].
- **PR Approval Policy:** Non-author approvals are required for all deliverables, and automated AI contributions require human maintainer engagement [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].

# Lifecycle History

Established under the AAIF technical committee. In September 2026, the group initiated alternate-week APAC timezone bridge meetings to improve cross-regional participation across Japan and other Asian time zones [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].

proposed_concept.title: Observability and Traceability Working Group
proposed_concept.description: AAIF technical working group establishing vendor-neutral agent telemetry standards, cross-boundary tracing specifications, and runtime observability reference architectures.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Observability and Traceability Working Group develops vendor-neutral agent telemetry specifications, semantic convention standards, and execution tracing patterns to enable monitoring and forensic visibility into multi-agent systems [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-59].

The group collaborates with [working-groups/security-and-privacy](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md) and [working-groups/identity-and-trust](../working-groups/identity-and-trust.md) to formulate cross-boundary audit logging and telemetry frameworks [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-3b2755238b15-1588e821].

# Architecture / Specification

### Reporting and Automation Pipeline

To fulfill Technical Committee reporting requirements without manual compilation overhead, the working group employs automated monthly metric aggregation [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-59]:

- **Automated Monthly Metrics Workflow:** Operates on the 1st of every month via GitHub Actions (`monthly-metrics.yml`), capturing issue and pull request activity updated or created during the previous monthly period [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-9373ed8bd5e2-54fdeb4c].
- **Issue-Metrics Integration:** Uses pinned actions (`github-community-projects/issue-metrics` and `peter-evans/create-issue-from-file`) to generate counts, open/close ratios, and time-to-first-response statistics, publishing the combined markdown report directly as an issue labeled `monthly-report` [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-9373ed8bd5e2-54fdeb4c, ^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-59].
- **Scoped Execution Privileges:** Restricts execution permissions to `issues: write` and `pull-requests: read` using the standard GITHUB_TOKEN [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-file-9373ed8bd5e2-54fdeb4c].

# Lifecycle History

Formed under the AAIF Technical Committee. In September 2026, adopted the automated issue metrics reporting process in response to Technical Committee feedback on completion tracking [^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-59].

proposed_concept.title: Security and Privacy Working Group
proposed_concept.description: AAIF technical working group establishing threat models, defensive architecture patterns, runtime sandboxing requirements, and security best practices for agentic AI.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Security and Privacy Working Group advances the Agentic AI Foundation's mission by establishing security and privacy as a shared discipline across the agentic AI ecosystem[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b33563055168-511b4a56]. It produces open threat models, taxonomy inputs, and defensive architecture patterns that providers, consumers, and peer working groups can adopt to share responsibility for trustworthy agentic systems[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b33563055168-511b4a56].

# Governance and Leadership

The working group operates under the technical governance of the AAIF Technical Committee[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d7a6875f36a3-5484c59b]. Working group chairs are appointed by Platinum and Gold members for fixed terms[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b33563055168-511b4a56]:

- **Chair:** Alex Frazer (Runlayer, term March 1, 2026 – January 31, 2027)[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b33563055168-511b4a56]
- **Co-Chair:** Junjie Bu (Google, term March 1, 2026 – January 31, 2027)[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b33563055168-511b4a56]

Meetings convene biweekly on Tuesdays at 10:00 AM US Pacific Time, with an alternating APAC-friendly time zone trial under active coordination[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b33563055168-511b4a56][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d7a6875f36a3-5484c59b]. All meetings, recordings, and minutes are archived on the Linux Foundation LFX platform[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b33563055168-511b4a56].

# Workstreams and Deliverables

The working group manages several active workstreams and published draft deliverables[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-a9e41c531556-11747157]:

- **[Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide](../guidelines/agentic-ai-security-best-practices.md):** Comprehensive operational and architectural guidance covering secrets management, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool invocation security, skill verification, and guardrails[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-a9e41c531556-11747157].
- **[Threat Modeling Gap Analysis](../resources/agentic-ai-threat-modeling-gap-analysis.md):** Evaluation of AI threat frameworks (OWASP, CSA MAESTRO, NIST AI RMF) relative to agent-specific risks such as tool manipulation, multi-agent persuasion, and prompt integrity[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-0e2b23067e13-ece26d85][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-a9e41c531556-11747157].
- **Taxonomy Contributions:** Foundational security and privacy definitions originated within this group were transitioned in June 2026 to the unified [Taxonomy and Landscape](../working-groups/taxonomy-and-landscape.md) cross-working-group initiative[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-a9e41c531556-11747157][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d7a6875f36a3-5484c59b].

Agent identity architecture and workload delegation protocols (such as SPIFFE/SVID and RFC 8693 token exchange) are coordinated directly with the [Identity and Trust Working Group](../working-groups/identity-and-trust.md)[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf].

proposed_concept.title: Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide
proposed_concept.description: Practical security guidance, failure patterns, and architectural controls across secrets management, tool invocation, guardrails, evaluations, and forensics.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide establishes actionable implementation standards and defensive controls for engineers deploying autonomous agents into production[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf]. Authored under the [Security and Privacy Working Group](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md) by Fernando Lucktemberg and Matthew Khouzam, the specification identifies recurring failure patterns across five core areas: secrets management, secure tool invocation, guardrails, evaluation frameworks, and post-incident forensics[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf].

Deep identity mechanisms—including SPIFFE/SVID workload attestations, RFC 8693 delegation-chain tokens, and UCAN capability models—are explicitly scoped to the [Identity and Trust Working Group](../working-groups/identity-and-trust.md) and integrated via cross-group checklists[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf].

# Architecture / Specification

The guideline pairs operational failure modes with enforceable architectural controls[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-22190b4c1053-5db87bbc]:

## Secrets Management
Static credentials and environment variables present high-risk attack surfaces prone to deserialization leaks and prompt extraction (e.g., CVE-2025-68664)[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf]. The guide mandates transitioning from stored static credentials to ephemeral attestations[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf]:
1. **Workload Identity:** Cloud provider OIDC workload tokens (AWS IRSA, GCP Workload Identity, Azure Managed Identity) providing automatically rotated, short-lived tokens without environment secrets[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-22190b4c1053-5db87bbc].
2. **Dynamic Secrets Engines:** Vault-issued ephemeral credentials scoped per operation with strict TTL expiry[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf].
3. **Network-Layer Injection:** Sidecar or proxy injection for legacy backend targets, ensuring runtime agents never hold credentials in context[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf].
4. **Confidential Computing:** Isolation via Intel SGX/TDX or AMD SEV-SNP with hardware-attested key release for high-sensitivity workloads, balancing 2–10% compute overhead against hypervisor trust boundaries[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-22190b4c1053-5db87bbc].

## Secure Tool Invocation
Tool integrations via Model Context Protocol (MCP) introduce risks including description poisoning (Unicode tag injection), rug-pull tool definition changes, cross-server shadowing, and prompt injection attacks[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf]. Recommended controls require[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-22190b4c1053-5db87bbc]:
- **Mandatory Pre-Deployment Verification:** Screening public repositories for recent activity (≥90 days), vetting against vulnerability registries, and running static scanners[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-22190b4c1053-5db87bbc].
- **Transport Security:** Requiring OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and RFC 8707 audience resource indicators for HTTP MCP servers; isolating local stdio servers inside unprivileged sandboxes[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf].
- **Mediation Gateways:** Deploying traffic mediation proxies such as [agentgateway](../resources/agentgateway.md) to log full request-response payloads, enforce per-tool authorization, and check runtime tool hash invariants[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-22190b4c1053-5db87bbc].
- **Skill Verification:** Tiered scanning of agent skills for undeclared external domain invocations, unvetted `eval()` calls, and Base64-obscured logic[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-22190b4c1053-5db87bbc].

# Lifecycle History

Draft v0.1 of the guide was created within the [Security and Privacy Working Group](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md) as Deliverable 4 of 5[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-b8b8567533b6-28cc0dbf]. It was refined across August and September 2026 before merging via PR #9, accompanied by an implementation feature matrix cross-referencing industry agent safety frameworks[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d7a6875f36a3-5484c59b][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-22190b4c1053-5db87bbc].

proposed_concept.title: Agentic AI Threat Modeling: Gap Analysis and Framework Design
proposed_concept.description: Threat modeling assessment evaluating CSA MAESTRO, OWASP, and NIST AI RMF against multi-agent, tool invocation, and delegation vulnerabilities.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Agentic AI Threat Modeling Gap Analysis is an ongoing research initiative and deliverable produced by the [Security and Privacy Working Group](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md)[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-0e2b23067e13-ece26d85][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-a9e41c531556-11747157]. Led by Alon Mazor (Ocean Security) and Fernando Lucktemberg (SAP), the deliverable evaluates whether existing AI security frameworks—specifically CSA MAESTRO, OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, and NIST AI RMF—adequately address threats unique to autonomous and multi-agent architectures[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-0e2b23067e13-ece26d85].

# Architecture / Specification

The analysis identifies distinct agentic attack vectors that conventional model-centric threat frameworks leave unaddressed or under-specified[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-0e2b23067e13-ece26d85]:

- **Multi-Agent Persuasion and Collusion:** Vulnerabilities arising when malicious or compromised agents iteratively persuade downstream subagents to bypass local constraints.
- **Tool Invocation Risks:** Exploits targeting dynamic protocol boundaries, tool description poisoning, and unvalidated parameter injection during remote function execution.
- **Delegated Authorization Boundaries:** Security gaps in identity propagation, token scoping, and capability handoffs across autonomous agent chains.
- **Supply Chain Integrity:** Verification requirements covering system prompt immutability, foundation model provenance, and runtime tool manifest attestations[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-0e2b23067e13-ece26d85].

Findings from the gap analysis serve as foundational inputs into the working group's defensive design patterns catalog and the [Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide](../guidelines/agentic-ai-security-best-practices.md)[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-0e2b23067e13-ece26d85].

# Lifecycle History

The workstream initiated drafting in July 2026 with contributions from across member organizations including Capsule, Ericsson, Global Payments, Huawei, IBM, Semiotic AI, SAP, and TELUS[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-0e2b23067e13-ece26d85][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d7a6875f36a3-5484c59b]. The working group maintains the document as an active deliverable draft targeted for broader Technical Committee and peer working group alignment[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-a9e41c531556-11747157][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-d7a6875f36a3-5484c59b].

proposed_concept.title: Agentic AI Security Best Practices
proposed_concept.description: Practical guidance, operational recommendations, and architectural control mappings for builders implementing agentic AI systems.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide provides practical, actionable implementation guidance for developers and operators building agentic AI systems[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-e24f19bec4ac-d0ff1066]. While design patterns address specific component architectures, this guideline structures defensive decision-making, offering concrete recommendations and pointers to established external security frameworks rather than re-deriving security baseline standards[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-e24f19bec4ac-d0ff1066].

The guide is governed within the [Security and Privacy Working Group](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md) as an active living document maintained through GitHub issues and pull requests, co-led by Fernando Lucktemberg (SAP) and Matthew Khouzam (Ericsson)[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-e24f19bec4ac-d0ff1066].

# Architecture / Specification

### Core Topic Domains

The best practices catalog targets six foundational operational and defensive areas[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-e24f19bec4ac-d0ff1066]:

1. **Secrets Management**: Isolation and ephemeral credential issuance preventing runtime leakage across agent context windows, prompt templates, and tool arguments.
2. **Secure Tool Invocation**: Principle of least privilege, input parameter validation, and execution controls around autonomous tool calls.
3. **Guardrails**: Model-level and prompt-level policy constraints enforcing boundaries against prompt injection, jailbreaks, and unintended delegation.
4. **Evaluation Frameworks**: Empirical validation methods and red-teaming harnesses assessing agent safety before deployment.
5. **Post-Incident Forensics**: Auditable logging, telemetry extraction, and execution tracing needed to investigate security regressions and unauthorized actions.
6. **Curated External Framework References**: Alignments with external industry standards from OWASP, CSA, and NIST AI RMF without duplicating existing work[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-e24f19bec4ac-d0ff1066].

### Governance and Maintenance

The guide is maintained in the working group's deliverables catalog under continuous peer review. In accordance with working group decisions, updates require approval from the designated workstream leads prior to integration[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-file-e24f19bec4ac-d0ff1066].

proposed_concept.title: AAIF Create Chapter Skill
proposed_concept.description: Automated chapter provisioning skill cloning TemplateCity Drive assets, executing OOXML rebranding, and calibrating map marker placement.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The `aaif-create-chapter` skill provisions and rebrands community chapter assets by cloning template resources in Google Drive and adjusting presentation metadata for localized AAIF community chapters[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49]. The underlying engine rebrands OOXML slide decks and applies coordinate transformations to position localized chapter map markers accurately across presentation templates[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49].

This operational workflow complements [Community Event Operations](../skills/community-event-operations.md) and adheres to AAIF visual presentation conventions defined in [Brand Guidelines](../guidelines/brand-guidelines.md)[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49].

# Architecture / Specification

### OOXML Rebrand Engine

The script `create_chapter.py` performs document rebranding at the paragraph level rather than per XML run[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49]. By concatenating individual text runs, applying regex substitutions, and writing the rebranded text into the initial run, the engine remains resilient against arbitrary run-splitting introduced by presentation software[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49]. Context-sensitive heuristic logic determines abbreviation casing based on surrounding terms, while keeping chapter slugs normalized[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49].

### Gall Stereographic Map Marker Projection

Slide marker placement is executed by `reposition_map_marker` using a fitted Gall Stereographic projection mapping latitude and longitude to slide pixel coordinates[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49]:

- `lon2x`: Linear transformation proportional to longitude.
- `lat2y`: Linear transformation in `(1 + √2/2) * tan(lat / 2)`.

The projection parameters were calibrated against Natural Earth 110m coastline datasets composited over base slide imagery, achieving a mean residual of 0.64 pixels[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49]. Offline rebranding mode (`--rebrand-local`) requires explicit coordinates to avoid external geocoding dependencies during automated testing and validation runs[^evt-community-events-file-0dc3d95afe1f-91fcca49].

proposed_concept.title: AAIF Audit Slack Skill
proposed_concept.description: Verification and audit skill reconciling community Slack channels, organizer permissions, and membership against central chapter records.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The `aaif-audit-slack` skill audits and reconciles communication channels across community Slack workspaces against canonical chapter rosters[^evt-community-events-file-2ca2907cf349-5ea9efbb]. It validates channel privacy settings, identifies unassigned or orphan channels, checks organizer authorization status, and surfaces data discrepancies between operational intake sheets and Slack runtime membership[^evt-community-events-file-2ca2907cf349-5ea9efbb].

The audit integrates into broader ecosystem workflows alongside [AAIF Create Chapter](../skills/aaif-create-chapter.md) and [Community Event Operations](../skills/community-event-operations.md)[^evt-community-events-file-2ca2907cf349-5ea9efbb].

# Architecture / Specification

### Organizer Audit Engine (`audit_organizers.py`)

The organizer engine cross-references the canonical Chapters List, accepted organizer intake records, and live Slack API endpoints (`conversations.list`, `conversations.members`, and `users.lookupByEmail`)[^evt-community-events-file-2ca2907cf349-5ea9efbb]:

- **Identity Reconciliation**: Organizers are matched between intake sheets and Slack accounts strictly via email addresses. Unmatched entries indicate an account discrepancy bound to email mismatches rather than definitive absence[^evt-community-events-file-2ca2907cf349-5ea9efbb].
- **Privilege Separation and Visibility**: The highest-severity finding surfaced by the audit is a public `-organizers` channel (`public!`), which risks exposing private venue budgets and operational logistics to the full workspace[^evt-community-events-file-2ca2907cf349-5ea9efbb].
- **Provisioning Lifecycle Flags**: The `--planned-ok` execution flag supports pre-provisioning workflows, downgrading anticipated rooms or private holding squats into non-aborting planned markers while channel setup scripts execute[^evt-community-events-file-2ca2907cf349-5ea9efbb].
- **Canonical Source Precedence**: The central Chapters List maintains exclusive authority over channel mapping; audit reports output discrepancy summaries without mutating mappings directly[^evt-community-events-file-2ca2907cf349-5ea9efbb].

proposed_concept.title: Agent Behavior Trace Model
proposed_concept.description: Standardized telemetry context and correlation framework capturing causal relationships, execution spans, and behavioral transitions in agent systems.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Agent Behavior Trace Model is an open standard and telemetry framework developed by the [Observability and Traceability Working Group](../working-groups/observability-and-traceability.md) to structure how AI agent actions, planning phases, and tool interactions are captured as standardized traces[^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-60]. By extending and mapping to [OpenTelemetry](../resources/opentelemetry.md) GenAI semantic conventions, the model defines consistent correlation semantics across multi-turn, multi-agent, and tool-augmented runs[^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-60].

# Architecture / Specification

### Execution Strategy: Evidence-First Model

Due to observed inconsistencies in how commercial and open-source agent frameworks implement OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, the working group restructured the trace model execution plan around empirical emission evidence rather than theoretical schema design[^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-60]. The model progresses across four iterative phases[^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-60]:

1. **Agree**: Establish baseline telemetry scope and target milestone boundaries.
2. **Evidence**: Capture and catalog real telemetry emitted by active agent runtimes into a shared gap register.
3. **Interpret**: Identify missing semantic primitives, unmapped causal chains, and lifecycle ambiguities across captured traces.
4. **Contribute**: Synthesize findings into concrete upstream OpenTelemetry proposals and AAIF semantic definitions.

### Reference Implementation

[Goose](../resources/goose.md), AAIF's open-source autonomous agent framework, serves as the primary initial reference implementation for capturing baseline traces and evaluating trace model compliance against real-world execution workloads[^evt-wg-observability-and-traceability-pr-60].

proposed_concept.title: Agent Plugin Portability Guidelines
proposed_concept.description: Packaging, runtime abstraction, and authorization guidelines ensuring agent skills and plugins execute reliably across diverse client harnesses.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Agent Plugin Portability Guidelines establish architectural standards, directory layouts, and execution boundaries that allow plugins and agent skills to run portably across client harnesses including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69] Rather than coupling plugins to client-specific configuration directories or tool implementations, portable plugins adopt canonical root manifests, capability abstractions, and standardized relative path references.[^evt-community-events-pr-54]

# Architecture / Specification

## Canonical Manifest Structure

Under the Agent Plugins v1 standard, the root `plugin.json` acts as the canonical manifest for common metadata, versioning, and capabilities.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69] When client-specific overlays are necessary, such as Claude Code's `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and marketplace catalog `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, they coexist alongside the root manifest without overriding core definitions.[^evt-community-events-pr-54] Repositories omit client-specific overlays (such as `.codex-plugin` or `.cursor-plugin`) when no client-specific components are configured.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69]

## Relative Pathing and Capability Abstraction

To ensure portability according to the [Agent Skills standard](../standards/agent-skills.md):
- **Relative paths**: Every file path inside a `SKILL.md` or its linked documents is relative to the directory containing that `SKILL.md`.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69]
- **`<skill-root>` placeholder**: Command examples replace client-specific variables (such as `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`) with the universal placeholder `<skill-root>`, which runtime agents resolve dynamically to the loaded skill directory.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69]
- **Capability declarations**: Skill workflows specify required underlying capabilities (e.g., reading files, running Python subprocesses, reading web pages, showing files, requesting human approval) rather than invoking proprietary client tool names.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69]
- **Namespaced metadata**: Non-standard frontmatter fields such as autocomplete hints are stored under namespaced string metadata rather than custom root fields, preventing syntax errors in standards-compliant parsers.[^evt-community-events-pr-54]

## Authorization and Mutation Boundaries

Loading or invoking an agent skill does not imply authorization to mutate external systems.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69] In alignment with the [Human Approval Gate pattern](../patterns/human-approval-gate.md):
- **Plan-by-default**: Diagnostic reports and execution plans are strictly read-only by default.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69]
- **Explicit mutation flags**: Mutating external state requires explicit operational flags (such as `--write`, `--apply`, or `--create`) passed only after explicit human review.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69]
- **Human gate flags**: Flags representing human authorization (such as `--i-have-approval`) must never be autonomously provided by an agent.[^evt-community-events-file-57c4a0921db3-7bd7bd69]
- **Secret hygiene**: Authentication credentials are provided strictly via environment variables, gitignored local configuration files, or system keychains, never passed on `argv` or embedded in prompt logs.[^evt-community-events-file-63a9c44a44ac-37822210]

## Automated Portability and Policy Enforcement

Continuous integration pipelines and pre-commit hooks enforce portability invariants across all skill definitions:[^evt-community-events-file-63a9c44a44ac-37822210][^evt-community-events-file-a5c0f08bc43f-b99183b6]
- Validating `plugin.json` against the [Agent Plugins standard](../standards/agent-plugins.md) and verifying `SKILL.md` frontmatter schemas.
- Rejecting proprietary client environment variables and hardcoded client tool references.
- Enforcing banner consistency across distributed skills to prevent instruction drift.
- Restricting credential access to gated workflow dispatch triggers, preventing fork workflows from exfiltrating credentials.[^evt-community-events-file-a5c0f08bc43f-b99183b6]

proposed_concept.title: AAIF Create Chapter Skill
proposed_concept.description: Automated chapter provisioning, backfill reconciliation, and four-surface renaming skill managing Google Drive assets, OOXML templates, and CRM data.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The AAIF Create Chapter skill automates chapter provisioning, estate-wide template backfills, and chapter renaming across Google Drive workspaces, OOXML presentation templates, and event tracking sheets.[^evt-community-events-file-799e4722911d-3d7dbf62][^evt-community-events-file-ec8a86dec4ad-08c3cbb3] The skill provides deterministic scripts and safe execution protocols that maintain synchronization between Drive assets, website event feeds, and presentation slide decks.[^evt-community-events-file-799e4722911d-3d7dbf62]

# Architecture / Specification

## Estate-Wide Backfill Operations

When global template assets, geographic projections, or roster entries change, the skill executes targeted backfill scripts across existing chapter decks:[^evt-community-events-file-799e4722911d-3d7dbf62]
- **Map Marker Synchronization (`backfill_map_dots.py`)**: Re-positions chapter location markers in existing slide decks using the Gall Stereographic projection.[^evt-community-events-file-799e4722911d-3d7dbf62] Coordinates are sourced strictly from the `Chapters & Teams` sheet joined to Google Drive via chapter folder URLs rather than folder names.[^evt-community-events-file-799e4722911d-3d7dbf62]
- **Footer and Project Rosters**: Updates host slide footers (`backfill_host_footer.py`) and project rosters (`backfill_projects.py`) across chapter templates via direct OOXML part surgery.[^evt-community-events-file-799e4722911d-3d7dbf62]
- **Plan-by-Default Execution**: All backfill scripts run in a plan-only mode by default, reporting drift across the estate before writing changes via `--write`.[^evt-community-events-file-799e4722911d-3d7dbf62]
- **Tolerance Checks**: Markers within a configured tolerance (default 1 px) are skipped to prevent redundant file rewrites and revision history churn.[^evt-community-events-file-799e4722911d-3d7dbf62]

## Four-Surface Chapter Renaming

Renaming an existing chapter is managed by `rename_chapter.py` and mandates synchronized modification across four distinct surfaces:[^evt-community-events-file-ec8a86dec4ad-08c3cbb3]
1. **Drive Chapter Folder**: The root folder name is renamed in Drive.
2. **File and Subfolder Names**: Nested CRM spreadsheets, assets, and folders are renamed.
3. **OOXML Document Text**: Text occurrences across `.docx`, `.pptx`, and `.xlsx` files are substituted.
4. **Document Metadata (`docProps`)**: Internal document properties and chapter metadata labels are updated.

### Renaming Invariants and Safety Controls

- **Platform Slug Decoupling**: Luma event platform slugs are decoupled from the chapter name; slugs are preserved unless explicitly passed with `--slug-from` and `--slug-to`, preventing 404 broken links when an external URL does not move with the city name.[^evt-community-events-file-ec8a86dec4ad-08c3cbb3]
- **Narrowed `.rels` Substitution**: In OOXML archives, `.rels` relationship parts only receive slug substitutions, preventing corrupted document targets if city substrings appear in file paths.[^evt-community-events-file-ec8a86dec4ad-08c3cbb3]
- **Automated Backup and Verification**: Original files are backed up to a timestamped backup directory before mutation, and post-write verification re-reads all files from Drive to verify no residual text or mismatched names remain.[^evt-community-events-file-ec8a86dec4ad-08c3cbb3]

# References

- Portability guidelines: [Agent Plugin Portability Guidelines](../guidelines/agent-plugin-portability.md)
- Human approval controls: [Human Approval Gate Pattern](../patterns/human-approval-gate.md)

proposed_concept.title: Agentic Use Case Classification Schema
proposed_concept.description: Twelve-column taxonomy separating structural design choices into five classification dimensions from seven supporting execution and evidence fields.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Agentic AI Foundation Workflows & Process Integration Working Group defines a standardized twelve-column classification schema for describing and comparing agentic workflows across production deployments [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-6cdd0fb97084-5ba45ebc]. Developed by the Critical Use Cases Workstream, the schema establishes a common framework to classify implementations in the companion use case inventory [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-pr-46].

The schema explicitly distinguishes between five core structural dimensions that reflect deliberate architectural choices and seven supporting fields that provide row identification, runtime observations, and empirical deployment evidence [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-6cdd0fb97084-5ba45ebc]. Workflows are classified against their specific cited implementations rather than abstract use case names, accommodating variations across systems sharing similar functional titles.

# Architecture / Specification

### Classification Dimensions

A classification dimension represents a structural fork in workflow design. The schema standardizes five discrete dimensions [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-6cdd0fb97084-5ba45ebc]:

1. **Trigger**: The invocation mechanism initiating workflow execution (external system events, scheduled cron routines, or direct human prompting).
2. **HITL Pattern**: The human-in-the-loop governance structure determining where, if anywhere, human intervention is mandatory before proceeding (e.g., [human approval gates](../patterns/human-approval-gate.md) or checkpoints).
3. **Agent Count**: The number of distinct reasoning agents deployed, driven by task decomposition, model specialization, or isolated tool privilege boundaries.
4. **Coordination**: The control mechanism orchestrating multi-agent or multi-step execution, categorized as fixed deterministic code or dynamic runtime model reasoning.
5. **Workflow Pattern**: The operational execution topology, distinguishing sequential straight-line executions, concurrent branch-and-merge pipelines, or iterative loops retrying against validation gates (such as [bounded convergence loops](../patterns/bounded-convergence-loop.md)).

### Supporting Fields

The remaining seven columns record non-dimensional metadata, observed metrics, and evidentiary rationale [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-6cdd0fb97084-5ba45ebc]:

- **Duration**: Empirical agent processing time, strictly excluding human approval queue waits and external downstream latency.
- **Use Case & Description**: Standardized names and descriptive summaries.
- **Tools & Systems**: Connected external interfaces and host environments.
- **Key Failure Mode**: Principal breakdown scenarios observed or mitigated.
- **Preconditions**: Required system states, tokens, or environment baselines.
- **Notes**: Rationale and verifiable deployment citations.

# Lifecycle History

The classification schema was developed within the Critical Use Cases Workstream and merged in pull request #46 [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-pr-46]. As of late 2026, the schema definitions and category groupings are positioned for Working Group review, with formal alignment underway with the Reference Architecture Workstream [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-6cdd0fb97084-5ba45ebc].

# References

- Companion catalog: [Agentic Use Case Inventory](../resources/agentic-use-case-inventory.md)
- Working group: [Workflows & Process Integration Working Group](../working-groups/workflows-and-process-integration.md)
- Architecture guidelines: [Workflow Pattern Template](../guidelines/workflow-pattern-template.md)

proposed_concept.title: Agentic Use Case Inventory
proposed_concept.description: Production workflow repository classifying real-world agent deployments under verified multi-tiered evidentiary standards.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Agentic Use Case Inventory is a curated repository of production agentic workflows maintained by the Critical Use Cases Workstream within the [Workflows & Process Integration Working Group](../working-groups/workflows-and-process-integration.md) [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-5028db4c24a1-b054a303]. Each entry documents an explicit, real-world implementation choice across varied industry verticals, serving as empirical evidence to identify recurring architectural patterns and workflow topologies [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-pr-46].

Workflows in the inventory are mapped against the five structural dimensions defined in the [Agentic Use Case Classification Schema](../resources/agentic-use-case-classification.md) [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-5028db4c24a1-b054a303].

# Architecture / Specification

### Evidentiary Standard

To ensure academic and operational rigor, all rows in the inventory must cite publicly accessible, independently verifiable proof of production deployment [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-5028db4c24a1-b054a303]. Unverifiable claims and personal assertions are explicitly disallowed. The workstream enforces a three-tier source qualification standard [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-5028db4c24a1-b054a303]:

1. **Preferred Sources**: Primary vendor product announcements or documentation confirming a named customer deployment operating in production (e.g., enterprise pairings demonstrating live utilization).
2. **Acceptable Sources**: Vendor product pages detailing explicit feature architectures clearly deployed at scale, even if specific customer identities are omitted.
3. **Unacceptable Sources**: Secondary blogs, analyst reports, market projection statistics, academic whitepapers, individual implementer blogs, and private knowledge.

Each inventory entry requires at least one verified primary citation, with three independent citations established as the operational target [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-5028db4c24a1-b054a303]. Technical guides and whitepapers may be used secondarily within classification notes to explain mechanics, provided they directly reference a qualified production vendor [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-5028db4c24a1-b054a303].

### Derivation of Workflow Shapes

The inventory enables the automated derivation of recurring workflow shapes by analyzing structural dimension frequencies across domains [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-file-5028db4c24a1-b054a303]. This empirical grounding allows the working group to prioritize reference architecture patterns based on demonstrated industry prevalence rather than speculative designs.

# Lifecycle History

Established under PR #46, the inventory structure and evidentiary rules achieved review readiness for Working Group approval in late 2026, with row-level citations undergoing continuous community verification [^evt-wg-workflows-and-process-integration-pr-46].

# References

- Companion schema: [Agentic Use Case Classification](../resources/agentic-use-case-classification.md)
- Working group: [Workflows & Process Integration Working Group](../working-groups/workflows-and-process-integration.md)

proposed_concept.title: Inherited Security Floor
proposed_concept.description: Architectural pattern enforcing consistent security baselines across heterogeneous agent surfaces through single-source policy declaration and transport inheritance.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview

The Inherited Security Floor pattern (also described as Declare–Pin–Inherit–Prove) provides an architectural approach to preventing policy drift across disparate agent exposure surfaces [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-29]. Rather than permitting individual transports—such as local tool servers, browser client tools, static task boards, or agent-to-agent interfaces—to maintain independent security definitions, systems implementing this pattern require every surface to inherit an immutable security floor declared in a centralized discovery manifest [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-29].

This pattern was submitted as a candidate design pattern to the [Security and Privacy Working Group](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md) to address divergence in safety rules across multi-transport deployments [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-29].

# Architecture / Specification

The pattern organizes agent interface security around four operational principles [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-29]:

1. **Unified Tool Contracts and Payload Strictness**: Heterogeneous transports expose identical tool signatures and argument types, guaranteeing value equivalence across protocols. Result payloads enforce fixed metadata fields (`source`, `trust`, `license`, `type`, and `body`), with the `trust` attribute permanently pinned to `untrusted`. Arguments strictly accept opaque entity identifiers rather than raw file paths, URLs, or shell strings.
2. **Human-Gated Consequential Writes**: Modifying actions are isolated behind reviewed proposals and [human approval gates](../patterns/human-approval-gate.md). Transports lacking configuration authority (such as client-side browser execution) are restricted to local-only operations and forbidden from direct network mutation.
3. **Peer Fetching and SSRF Protection**: Inbound and outbound peer federation is constrained to HTTPS endpoints checked against IANA special-purpose address denial lists. The runtime enforces hop, fan-out, and redirect limits, re-verifying socket remote IP addresses post-connection to defeat DNS rebinding attacks.
4. **Static State Export**: Multi-agent boards (such as [agent-to-agent](../taxonomy/agent-to-agent.md) coordination boards) are published as immutable static files reflecting engine states verbatim, allowing peer consumption without exposing writable execution surfaces.

# Lifecycle History

Proposed in issue #29 within the AAIF Security and Privacy Working Group as candidate input for open threat models and design pattern deliverables [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-29]. It remains a draft community proposal pending formal alignment and working group consensus.

# References

- Security guidance: [Agentic AI Security Best Practices](../guidelines/agentic-ai-security-best-practices.md)
- Approval controls: [Human Approval Gate](../patterns/human-approval-gate.md)
- Governance: [Security and Privacy Working Group](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md)

proposed_concept.title: Agentic AI Security Best Practices
proposed_concept.description: Practical security controls and feature requirement mappings across people, process, and technology pillars for agentic AI deployments.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview
Agentic AI Security Best Practices establishes operational guidelines, architectural controls, and defensive practices for organizations engineering and deploying autonomous agent systems. Authored by the Security and Privacy Working Group (../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md), the guidance provides an actionable baseline to safeguard agent execution boundaries, tool interfaces, and sensitive data flows.

# Architecture / Specification
The framework maps every recommended security best practice against the specific features required to enforce it, categorizing operational requirements into three core dimensions [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-pr-20]:

- **People**: Capabilities requiring specialized skills, personnel training, security awareness education, and human oversight across design and operational lifecycles.
- **Process**: Organizational governance requiring documented policies, standardized operational procedures, risk management reviews, and formal compliance strategies.
- **Technology**: Concrete technical tooling, hardware-backed isolation, automated policy enforcement mechanisms, runtime guardrails, and cryptographic controls.

This matrix ensures that defensive architectures do not rely exclusively on runtime technological filters, but are reinforced by procedural governance and organizational readiness.

# Lifecycle History
The baseline security practices were originally established by the Security and Privacy Working Group to complement agent threat modeling efforts. PR #20 introduced the comprehensive feature support matrix linking each best practice to concrete people, process, and technology capabilities [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-pr-20].

# Overview
The Blog Guidelines set editorial standards, intake requirements, and review processes for articles published on the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) blog. The guideline instructs contributors on tone, structure, factual attribution, and branding alignment to ensure objective, high-quality technical publications across the foundation's public channels.

# Architecture / Specification
Blog content submitted for publication must conform to key editorial and stylistic invariants [^evt-foundation-pr-7]:

- **Typography and Casing**: Headers and section titles follow standard sentence case conventions.
- **Language and Spelling**: Content must be written in standard US English.
- **Evidentiary Claims**: Categorical claims must not be unsupported; technical assertions require empirical justification or explicit boundary caveats.
- **Attribution and Primary Sources**: References must link directly to authoritative primary sources rather than secondary aggregators or promotional summaries.
- **Project Naming**: Technical projects, foundation bodies, and open-source specifications must utilize official, canonical naming without marketing inflation.

Contributors authoring content are encouraged to consult ../skills/aaif-blog-guidelines.md for automated validation and workflow checks prior to submitting publication proposals.

# Lifecycle History
Maintained by foundation operations, these guidelines ensure consistent technical and editorial voice across all AAIF communication platforms. PR #7 updated the guidelines to formalize sentence case, US English spelling, strict primary-source linking, and official project naming criteria [^evt-foundation-pr-7].

proposed_concept.title: Community Event Operations
proposed_concept.description: Procedural orchestration pipeline and synchronization engine enforcing non-destructive chapter deprecation and human drift resolution.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview
Community Event Operations provides automated operational tooling and scripts for managing Agentic AI Foundation events, chapter rosters, and sync pipelines. The skill governs data reconciliation across spreadsheets and public listings, enforcing strict safeguards against data loss while highlighting administrative discrepancies for human review.

# Architecture / Specification
The chapter synchronization pipeline (`sync_chapters.py`) enforces a non-destructive lifecycle invariant where chapter rows are never cleared or deleted automatically [^evt-community-events-pr-55]:

- **Retirement Candidates**: When a chapter city lacks a qualifying active organizer, the sync engine flags the record as a retirement candidate via `retirement_candidates()` instead of clearing row contents. This protects handwritten fields such as summaries, operational notes, and asset links.
- **Ambiguity Holds**: The engine skips rows already marked as `Deprecated` or `Merged`, and holds candidate processing if organizer data contains ambiguous near-misses, malformed city values, or unassigned records already listed.
- **Human Drift Resolution**: Candidates are posted to the synchronization run's Drift tab for human intervention. To finalize retirement, an administrator manually sets `Status=Deprecated` or configures `Status=Merged` with an explicit `Merged Into` target.
- **Zero-Write Deletion**: The write path (`apply_changes`) excludes removal arguments, and candidate reporting leaves execution exit codes neutral to prevent spurious CI build failures.

# Lifecycle History
In PR #55, the synchronization architecture was altered after dry runs revealed that automated row clearing risked deleting valid shadow chapters and recently renamed city locations; candidate quarantine was implemented in place of row removal [^evt-community-events-pr-55].

The Accuracy and Reliability Working Group (ARWG) is an AAIF technical body focused on defining metrics, benchmarks, and engineering standards for evaluating agentic AI correctness and dependability. The group develops quantitative testing frameworks and diagnostic instruments such as the ../resources/accuracy-and-reliability-survey.md to measure failure modes in autonomous pipelines.

# Architecture / Specification

- **Deliverable 1 (D1)**: Specification covering failure categorization, accuracy grading methods, and evaluation baselines.
- **Deliverable 2 (D2)**: The community deployment and reliability survey assessing production failure topologies and readiness levels.
- **Cross-Group Coordination**: Alignment with ../working-groups/observability-and-traceability.md and ../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md for joint verification pipelines.

# Lifecycle History
Operating under the AAIF Technical Committee (../governance/technical-committee.md), ARWG conducts regular review cycles on core deliverables. In the August 2026 report (PR #10), the working group completed the review cycle for the D2 survey (PR #9), advanced D1 review milestones (PR #8), addressed review questions from the prior July period, and commenced cross-working-group preparations for Phase 2 operations [^evt-wg-accuracy-and-reliability-pr-10].

proposed_concept.title: Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide
proposed_concept.description: Actionable security controls, threat mitigations, and framework alignments across agent lifecycles, execution boundaries, and credential hygiene.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview
The Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide provides an operational security baseline for deploying and managing autonomous agents and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool integrations. Maintained by the [Security and Privacy Working Group](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md), the guide specifies defensive patterns across identity, sandbox execution, context boundary isolation, and behavioral monitoring.

# Architecture / Specification
The framework addresses architectural vulnerability domains across agent communication channels and runtime environments:

## In-Loop Hook vs. Gateway Mediation
While centralized API and MCP gateways provide external ingress mediation, mutual authentication, and centralized telemetry capture, critical runtime enforcement requires in-loop execution hooks inside the agent runtime loop.[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-30] In-loop hooks inspect tool calls before invocation across transports—including local stdio subprocesses, direct Python or Node SDK calls, and shell commands that bypass network proxies—enabling prompt-aware, context-sensitive access control.[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-30]

## Credential and Secret Boundary Defense
Defensive baselines require auditing and isolating secrets across three vulnerable surfaces:[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-33]
- **Configuration & Skill Artifacts**: Auditing agent configuration manifests (`.mcp.json`, client configs) and skill bundles to prevent committing hardcoded tokens or environment keys.[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-33]
- **Context & Memory Leakage**: Redacting sensitive tool outputs before values enter the context window, prompt transcripts, trace logs, or persistent memory systems to eliminate memory-based privilege retention.[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-33]
- **Host & Environment Isolation**: Restricting file system access via strict deny rules at execution hooks against host credential paths (`~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, browser session caches) and mandating short-lived credential exchange to mitigate sandbox escape risks.[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-33]

## Threat Framework Alignments
The guide's threat catalog and operational controls align against standardized industry risk taxonomies, specifically MITRE ATLAS technique codes (such as AML.T0110 for Tool Poisoning, AML.T0055 for Unsecured Credentials, and AML.T0086 for Tool Exfiltration) and OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI) risk categories.[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-32]

# Lifecycle History
Derived from the initial security guide draft developed under PR #9 of the Security and Privacy Working Group, with ongoing proposals refining execution-layer policy hooks, credential hygiene scopes, and formal ATLAS/ASI mapping matrices.[^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-30][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-32][^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-33]

proposed_concept.title: Agentic AI Security Best Practices
proposed_concept.description: Actionable security controls, threat mitigations, and execution boundary standards across agent lifecycles, tool execution environments, and sandbox deployments.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview
The Agentic AI Security Best Practices guide establishes actionable defensive patterns, runtime isolation baselines, and execution boundary controls for autonomous agent systems. It provides engineering teams and enterprise operators with prescriptive guidance to evaluate, sandbox, and monitor agent tooling and privileged actions.

Under active review by the Security & Privacy Working Group, the guide addresses the practical boundaries of agent sandboxing, warning against relying on local execution sandboxes as complete security perimeters [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-34].

# Architecture / Specification
The guidelines define defensive security controls across agent execution layers, emphasizing the operational boundaries of isolated execution:

## Sandbox Containment and Blast Radius
Runtime sandboxing is recommended for unverified agent tool invocations, but working group evaluations clarify that sandbox modes narrow local filesystem scope rather than fully containing arbitrary code execution [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-34]:
- **Filesystem Constraints**: Sandboxing restricts access to designated working directories, preventing unauthorized reads or writes across broader system directories [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-34].
- **Egress and Network Leakage**: Standard execution sandboxes frequently leave network egress open; agents can utilize unblocked runtime utilities (such as Python's standard `urllib`) to exfiltrate project files to public hosts even when CLI utilities like `curl` are filtered [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-34].
- **Host Tool Handoffs**: Sandbox boundaries can be circumvented without breaking isolation if an agent writes malicious instructions or generated code to disk that is subsequently run by an unsandboxed host process or tool [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-34].
- **Hardware-Attested Alternatives**: For strict verification requirements, environments should pair isolation controls with patterns like [Attested Isolated Runtime](../patterns/attested-isolated-runtime.md) rather than relying solely on user-space directory chroots.

# Lifecycle History
The guide was drafted within the Security & Privacy Working Group. Ongoing revisions refine Section 3.2 to adjust ratings from full system containment to explicit filesystem narrowing, addressing real-world sandbox escape vectors and egress circumvention [^evt-wg-security-and-privacy-issue-34].

proposed_concept.title: Identity and Trust Working Group
proposed_concept.description: AAIF technical working group establishing vendor-neutral architectures, delegation models, attestation specifications, and identity frameworks for autonomous agents.
proposed_concept.body:
# Overview
The Identity and Trust Working Group establishes vendor-neutral architectures, delegation models, identity frameworks, and hardware attestation mechanisms for autonomous AI agents. The working group's charter covers identity issuance, cryptographic attestation, authentication, delegation chains, and authorization standards across heterogeneous multi-agent systems [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12].

# Architecture / Specification
The working group's reference architecture separates agent attestation into three distinct structural components to bridge hardware security primitives with agent runtime identities [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12]:

## Attestation Reference Model
1. **Platform Evidence**: Signed hardware or firmware reports and their cryptographic endorsement chains that measure and certify the physical or virtual execution environment [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12].
2. **Identity Binding**: Signed statements explicitly linking an agent's public identifier or cryptographic key to the platform evidence. Depending on runtime architecture, this binding traverses platform-specific channels [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12]:
   - *AMD SEV-SNP (e.g., GCP N2D)*: Guest environments populate the 64-byte `REPORT_DATA` directly with the agent identity digest [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12].
   - *Azure Confidential VMs (SEV-SNP and Intel TDX)*: The hardware `report_data` hashes a paravisor-constructed Runtime Claims document containing the vTPM AK public key, VM settings, and 64 bytes of guest `user-data` [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12].
   - *Accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA H100)*: Dedicated GPU attestation reports with independent nonces tied cryptographically back to the host CPU environment [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12].
3. **Appraisal**: Policy-driven evaluations performed by relying parties against appraisal criteria to emit an authorization or admission verdict [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12].

This separation coordinates with the runtime isolation models defined in [Attested Isolated Runtime](../patterns/attested-isolated-runtime.md) and security baselines overseen by the [Security and Privacy Working Group](../working-groups/security-and-privacy.md) [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12].

# Lifecycle History
Formed as a core technical working group within the Agentic AI Foundation. Technical proposals have focused on resolving platform discrepancies in confidential VM attestation and disambiguating hardware evidence from agent identity bindings [^evt-wg-identity-and-trust-issue-12].
